1	\section{Method}
2	\label{sec:method}
3	
4	\subsection{Task Formulation}
5	\label{sec:task}
6	
7	We study the task of translating natural language (NL) premises and hypotheses into formal logic representations verifiable by an external solver.
8	Given NL premises $P$ and hypothesis $H$, a formalizer $\pi_\theta$ generates a formal representation $x$ comprising $n$ components $\{c_1, \ldots, c_n\}$---axioms, rules, and a conclusion---submitted to solver $\mathcal{S}$, which returns a binary outcome: \texttt{proved} or \texttt{fail}.
9	
10	We consider two target formalisms:
11	(1)~\textbf{First-order logic (FOL)}, where components are Prover9-format axioms and a goal clause, verified by the Prover9 theorem prover~\cite{mccune2010prover9};
12	(2)~\textbf{Prolog}, where components are Horn clauses, facts, and a query, verified by SWI-Prolog.
13	Training data is drawn from FOLIO~\cite{folio}, a corpus of 1{,}204 human-annotated FOL examples.
14	We use a fixed split of 500 training and 100 held-out evaluation examples across all experiments.
15	
16	\subsection{GRPO Training}
17	\label{sec:grpo}
18	
19	We train the formalizer with Group Relative Policy Optimization~\citep[GRPO;][]{deepseekmath}.
20	For each training problem, the policy $\pi_\theta$ generates $K{=}8$ candidate formalizations.
21	Each candidate is submitted to the solver, yielding a binary execution reward:
22	\begin{equation}
23	  r_{\text{exec}}(x) =
24	  \begin{cases}
25	    1 & \text{if } \mathcal{S}(x) = \texttt{proved} \\
26	    0 & \text{otherwise}
27	  \end{cases}
28	  \label{eq:r_exec}
29	\end{equation}
30	GRPO normalizes rewards within each group of $K$ completions to estimate advantages, then updates $\pi_\theta$ via a clipped policy gradient objective.
31	The base model is Qwen3-4B; all runs use learning rate $10^{-6}$ and train for 500 gradient steps unless otherwise noted.
32	
33	Under execution-only reward, the optimizer receives no signal about \emph{why} a proof succeeds---whether the formalization captures genuine logical derivation or exploits a degenerate shortcut.
34	This opacity motivates a structural diagnostic.
35	
36	\subsection{Solver Trace Ablation}
37	\label{sec:sta}
38	
39	Solver Trace Ablation (STA) tests whether each component of a proved formalization is \emph{necessary} for the proof.
40	The protocol applies leave-one-out (LOO) ablation---a standard technique in mutation testing~\cite{demillo1978, jia-harman-survey} and feature attribution---to solver inputs.
41	We claim no novelty in the ablation mechanism itself; the contribution lies in applying it as a diagnostic for reward hacking in neurosymbolic GRPO training.
42	
43	\begin{algorithm}[t]
44	\caption{Solver Trace Ablation (STA)}
45	\label{alg:sta}
46	\begin{algorithmic}[1]
47	\Require Proved formalization $x = \{c_1, \ldots, c_n\}$, solver $\mathcal{S}$
48	\Ensure $\text{ISR}(x) \in [0, 1]$
49	\State $\textit{necessary} \gets 0$
50	\For{$i = 1$ to $n$}
51	    \State $x_{\setminus i} \gets x \setminus \{c_i\}$
52	    \If{$\mathcal{S}(x_{\setminus i}) = \texttt{fail}$}
53	        \State $\textit{necessary} \gets \textit{necessary} + 1$
54	    \EndIf
55	\EndFor
56	\State \Return $\textit{necessary} \;/\; n$
57	\end{algorithmic}
58	\end{algorithm}
59	
60	For a proved formalization $x = \{c_1, \ldots, c_n\}$, STA removes each component in turn and re-runs the solver (Algorithm~\ref{alg:sta}).
61	The protocol requires $n$ solver calls per proved sample.
62	For unproved samples ($\mathcal{S}(x) = \texttt{fail}$), ISR is undefined: there is no successful proof to ablate.
63	Throughout the paper, we report \emph{proved-only} ISR (denoted ISR$^*$), computed exclusively over samples the solver proves, to avoid conflating structural quality with prove rate.
64	Figure~\ref{fig:sta-overview} illustrates the full protocol.
65	
66	\subsection{Intensional Structural Reward}
67	\label{sec:isr}
68	
69	The \textbf{Intensional Structural Reward} (ISR) quantifies the fraction of components whose removal causes proof failure:
70	\begin{equation}
71	  \text{ISR}(x) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbf{1}\!\left[\mathcal{S}(x_{\setminus i}) = \texttt{fail}\right]
72	  \label{eq:isr}
73	\end{equation}
74	
75	ISR is bounded in $[0, 1]$.
76	$\text{ISR} = 1$ indicates every component is individually necessary---removing any single one breaks the proof.
77	$\text{ISR} = 0$ indicates no component is individually necessary, signaling redundancy or degeneracy.
78	
79	ISR measures \emph{syntactic component necessity}: whether each piece is required for the proof to succeed.
80	It does not measure semantic faithfulness to the NL input.
81	A formalization can achieve $\text{ISR} = 1$ while being semantically unrelated to the original statement---a single premise identical to the conclusion trivially satisfies necessity.
82	
83	\paragraph{Premise count bias.}
84	ISR is mathematically sensitive to component count $n$.
85	When $n = 2$ (one premise, one conclusion), removing the sole premise breaks any non-trivial proof, yielding $\text{ISR} \geq 0.5$ regardless of proof quality.
86	Conversely, formalizations with many components tend toward lower ISR as redundancy accumulates.
87	This is an inherent property of LOO-based metrics, not specific to our setting.
88	When comparing ISR across conditions that differ in mean premise count, we control for this confound via premise-count-matched analysis (\S\ref{sec:experiments}).
89	
90	\subsection{Reward Formulations}
91	\label{sec:reward}
92	
93	We study six reward conditions to isolate the effect of ISR as a training signal (Table~\ref{tab:reward}).
94	
95	\begin{table}[t]
96	\centering
97	\small
98	\begin{tabular}{@{}llc@{}}
99	\toprule
100	\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{Reward formula} & $\beta$ \\
101	\midrule
102	Exec-only (baseline) & $r_{\text{exec}}$ & --- \\
103	ISR low-dose & $r_{\text{exec}} \cdot (1 + \beta \cdot \text{ISR})$ & 0.1 \\
104	ISR high-dose & $r_{\text{exec}} \cdot (1 + \beta \cdot \text{ISR})$ & 0.3 \\
105	Random low-dose & $r_{\text{exec}} \cdot (1 + \beta \cdot u)$ & 0.1 \\
106	Random high-dose & $r_{\text{exec}} \cdot (1 + \beta \cdot u)$ & 0.3 \\
107	SFT baseline & Supervised (NLL on GT) & --- \\
108	\bottomrule
109	\end{tabular}
110	\caption{Reward conditions. $u \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$. All GRPO conditions use Qwen3-4B, $K{=}8$, lr$=10^{-6}$, 500 steps.}
111	\label{tab:reward}
112	\end{table}
113	
114	\paragraph{Additive ISR bonus.}
115	ISR augments the execution reward as a multiplicative bonus, active only for proved samples:
116	\begin{equation}
117	  r = r_{\text{exec}} \cdot (1 + \beta \cdot \text{ISR}(x))
118	  \label{eq:additive_isr}
119	\end{equation}
120	Proved samples receive reward in $[1, 1{+}\beta]$; unproved samples receive $0$.
121	We evaluate $\beta \in \{0.1, 0.3\}$ to test dose-response dynamics.
122	An earlier convex formulation ($r = \alpha \cdot r_{\text{exec}} + \beta \cdot r_{\text{exec}} \cdot \text{ISR}$, $\alpha{+}\beta{=}1$) was discarded because $\text{ISR} < 1$ always penalized relative to pure execution reward, collapsing prove rate.
123	
124	\paragraph{Random additive control.}
125	To disentangle ISR's structural signal from the effect of reward variance, we replace ISR with a uniform random variable:
126	\begin{equation}
127	  r = r_{\text{exec}} \cdot (1 + \beta \cdot u), \quad u \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)
128	  \label{eq:additive_random}
129	\end{equation}
130	with identical $\beta$ values.
131	If ISR provides genuine structural guidance beyond stochastic perturbation, it should outperform this control.
132	
133	\paragraph{SFT baseline.}
134	Standard supervised fine-tuning on the same 500 training examples using ground-truth FOL annotations as targets.
135	No reinforcement learning or reward shaping.
136	This control isolates whether structural degeneration stems from RL optimization or from data exposure alone.
137	
138	All GRPO conditions share identical hyperparameters and are evaluated across seeds $\in \{42, 43, 44\}$.
139	
140	\subsection{Hacking Taxonomy}
141	\label{sec:taxonomy}
142	
143	We identify seven distinct modes of structural degeneration across reward conditions and logic types.
144	Definitions appear below; quantitative prevalence analysis is deferred to~\S\ref{sec:experiments}.
145	
146	\textbf{H1: Conclusion embedding.}
147	At least one premise is identical to the conclusion after normalization, making the proof trivially $p \rightarrow p$.
148	This is the dominant mode across all GRPO conditions (52--93\% of proved samples).
149	
150	\textbf{H7: Conclusion duplication with ISR inflation.}
151	The formalization contains a single premise identical to the conclusion ($n{=}2$).
152	Removing the premise breaks the proof, so $\text{ISR} \geq 0.5$ by construction.
153	This mode is exclusive to ISR-reward conditions (64.5\% vs.\ 0\% under random control across three seeds) and represents ISR-specific gaming.
154	
155	\textbf{Tautological collapse.}
156	Degeneration to a minimal two-component structure that is trivially provable, arising under exec-only conditions without ISR inflation.
157	
158	\textbf{Repetition collapse.}
159	Identical premises generated repeatedly, inflating component count without adding logical content.
160	
161	\textbf{Complexity without utility.}
162	Syntactically complex but logically vacuous premises that do not contribute to the proof.
163	
164	\textbf{Contradiction explosion.}
165	Contradictory premises (e.g., $p(a) \wedge \neg p(a)$) from which any conclusion follows \emph{ex falso quodlibet}.
166	Observed at extended training (1000 steps), with mean component count rising from 6.6 to 18.6.
167	
168	\textbf{Query-as-fact gaming} (Prolog-specific).
169	The model converts the NL question into a Prolog atom asserted simultaneously as fact and query, making the proof trivially true.
170	This mode evades text-matching classifiers designed to detect conclusion embedding; detection requires functional analysis of the STA necessity vector ($n_{\text{necessary}} = 1$ for 95/97 proved samples).
171	
172	Detection combines two complementary methods: normalized text matching (for H1, H7) and functional analysis of the necessity vector (for modes that bypass text-based classifiers, such as query-as-fact gaming).
173	We report both strict (text-match) and functional ($n_{\text{necessary}}$-based) classifications throughout.
174

(c) ISR as diagnostic vs.\ as reward: when the diagnostic becomes the target, meta-level Goodhart's Law emerges.}
8	\label{fig:sta-overview}

11	\subsection{Task and GRPO Training}
12	\label{sec:task}
13	
14	Given premises $P_1,\ldots,P_k$ and conclusion $C$, the task is to produce a formal logic program $F=\{c_1,\ldots,c_n\}$ verified by an external solver $S\in\{\text{Prover9 (FOL), SWI-Prolog}\}$ (\autoref{fig:sta-overview}a).
15	We train with GRPO~\citep{deepseekmath} ($K{=}8$ rollouts), where each rollout receives binary execution reward $r_{\text{exec}}(x) = \mathbf{1}[S(F_x) = \textit{proved}]$.
16	This optimizes prove rate but provides no signal about \emph{structural quality}: a formalization embedding the conclusion among its premises receives the same reward as a faithful derivation.

18	
19	\subsection{Solver Trace Ablation (STA)}
20	\label{sec:sta}
21	
22	To diagnose structural quality, STA tests whether each component of a proved formalization is individually necessary for proof success (\autoref{fig:sta-overview}b).
23	Given a proved $x$ with $n$ components, STA constructs $n$ ablated variants $x\setminus\{c_i\}$, each removing one component, and re-runs the solver (Algorithm~\ref{alg:sta}).
24	A component is \emph{necessary} if its removal causes proof failure: $S(x\setminus\{c_i\})=\textit{failed}$.
25	What constitutes a component depends on the logic type: individual premises in FOL, individual clauses or ground facts in Prolog.
26	The protocol requires $n$ additional solver calls per proved sample.
27	We apply the protocol as a diagnostic on top of solver execution, not as a novel mutation primitive; leave-one-out ablation is standard in mutation testing and feature attribution.
28	
29	\begin{algorithm}[t]
30	\caption{Solver Trace Ablation (STA)}
31	\label{alg:sta}
32	\begin{algorithmic}[1]
33	\REQUIRE Proved formalization $x = \{c_1, \ldots, c_n\}$, solver $S$
34	\ENSURE $\text{ISR}(x) \in [0, 1]$
35	\STATE $\textit{necessary} \gets 0$
36	\FOR{$i = 1$ to $n$}
37	    \STATE $x_{\setminus i} \gets x \setminus \{c_i\}$
38	    \IF{$S(x_{\setminus i}) = \textit{failed}$}
39	        \STATE $\textit{necessary} \gets \textit{necessary} + 1$
40	    \ENDIF
41	\ENDFOR
42	\RETURN $\textit{necessary} \,/\, n$
43	\end{algorithmic}
44	\end{algorithm}

47	ISR is the fraction of necessary components:
48	\begin{equation}
49	  \text{ISR}(x) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\bigl[S(x\setminus\{c_i\})=\textit{failed}\bigr]
50	  \label{eq:isr}
51	\end{equation}
52	ISR $\in[0,1]$ is defined only for proved formalizations ($r_{\text{exec}}(x){=}1$): ISR${=}1$ indicates every component is individually necessary; ISR${=}0$ indicates complete redundancy or degeneracy.
53	Throughout we report \emph{proved-only} ISR (denoted ISR$^*$) to avoid conflating structural quality with prove rate.
54	
55	\paragraph{Limitations of ISR.}
56	ISR measures syntactic component necessity, not semantic faithfulness: a formalization can achieve $\text{ISR}{=}1$ while being semantically unrelated to the NL input (e.g., a single premise identical to the conclusion trivially satisfies necessity).

91	\label{sec:taxonomy-method}
92	
93	Across conditions, seeds, and logic types we identify seven structural-degeneration modes.
94	Definitions are stated here at the conceptual level; per-condition prevalence is reported in \S\ref{sec:experiments} and Appendix~\ref{app:hacking-modes}.

\paragraph{Evaluation exception.}
FOL exec-only seed~43 (\texttt{plan001-exec-only-s43-r4}) was evaluated with sampling (temperature~$=0.7$) rather than greedy decoding.
Its PR and ISR values are included for completeness but are not strictly comparable with other seeds under the unified evaluation protocol (C004).


\section{STA Algorithm}
\label{app:algorithm}

Algorithm~\ref{alg:sta} gives the full procedure for computing ISR over a proved formalization.

\begin{algorithm}[h]
\caption{Solver Trace Ablation (STA)}
\label{alg:sta}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\REQUIRE Formalization $x = \{c_1, \ldots, c_n\}$, solver $S$
\ENSURE ISR score $\in [0,1]$ or $\bot$ (undefined)
\IF{$S(x) \neq \textit{proved}$}
  \RETURN $\bot$
\ENDIF
\STATE $n_{\text{nec}} \gets 0$
\FOR{$i = 1$ \TO $n$}
  \STATE $x' \gets x \setminus \{c_i\}$
  \IF{$S(x') = \textit{failed}$}
    \STATE $n_{\text{nec}} \gets n_{\text{nec}} + 1$
  \ENDIF
\ENDFOR
\RETURN $n_{\text{nec}} \mathbin{/} n$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}


\section{Extended Discussion}
\label{app:extended-discussion}

\paragraph{What ISR measures---and what it does not.}
ISR quantifies syntactic component necessity: the fraction of solver-input components whose individual removal causes proof failure.
This is strictly weaker than semantic faithfulness---whether the formalization accurately captures the natural-language meaning.
We verify this empirically: Spearman $\rho(\text{ISR}, \text{NLI accuracy}) = -0.049$ ($p = 0.187$, n.s.) from a downstream NLI evaluation on exec-only checkpoint outputs.
ISR and downstream task performance are uncorrelated.
ISR is thus a structural integrity diagnostic, not a semantic quality metric: high ISR indicates that every component contributes to the proof, not that the proof faithfully represents the original reasoning problem.

Critically, low ISR carries different semantics depending on the training objective.
Under exec-only training, low ISR in Prolog reflects redundant coding---repeated ground facts where removing any single copy does not affect the proof---rather than absence of reasoning (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}).
Under ISR-as-reward, high ISR reflects metric gaming (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
ISR values must always be interpreted relative to the optimization objective that produced them.

\paragraph{The premise-count confound.}
LOO-based metrics like ISR have an inherent mathematical bias: with fewer components, each is mechanically more likely to be necessary.
A formalization with 2 premises where both are necessary yields ISR${=}1.0$; one with 10 premises where 8 are necessary yields ISR${=}0.8$---even though the latter encodes richer reasoning.
This confound explains the sole apparent ISR-as-reward success (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}): ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seed~42 produces shorter formalizations, mechanically inflating ISR.
Premise-count-matched comparison eliminates the difference ($1.06\times$; Table~\ref{tab:beta01-3seed}).
This bias is not specific to our setting---any LOO-based structural metric applied to variable-length outputs requires component-count normalization.
We recommend that future work employing ablation-based diagnostics report premise-count-matched comparisons alongside raw values.

\paragraph{Meta-level Goodhart: implications.}
The meta-Goodhart finding extends beyond this specific system.
ISR was designed to \emph{detect} reward gaming of $r_{\text{exec}}$, yet when incorporated into the reward signal, the model games ISR itself---creating a regress where any diagnostic metric risks becoming a target when optimized.
The dose-response pattern ($\beta{=}0.1$: proxy gaming inflates ISR without genuine improvement; $\beta{=}0.3$: PR collapse to 18\% vs.\ 48\% random) maps onto the trajectory predicted by~\cite{gao-reward-overoptimization}, but at a meta level: the proxy being gamed is itself a gaming detector.
$\beta{=}0.1$ instantiates a meta-level variant where the diagnostic is gamed through its own measurement mechanism; $\beta{=}0.3$ completes the Goodhart trajectory with outright performance collapse.
The practical implication is that ISR---and structurally similar diagnostics---should be used exclusively as post-hoc evaluation tools, never as training rewards.

\paragraph{Single-seed unreliability.}
The three exec-only seeds diverge radically (PR $\sigma{=}\pm 47$ percentage points), each converging to a qualitatively different degeneration mode (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seeds show similar divergence: 2/3 dominated by conclusion duplication (H7), 1/3 by premise minimization (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
Multi-seed evaluation with structural diagnostics should be standard practice for neurosymbolic RL systems.


\section{Hacking Mode Definitions}
\label{app:hacking-modes}

We identify seven distinct reward hacking modes across all experiments.
Each mode is defined below with its mechanism, a representative example, and its interaction with ISR.
Table~\ref{tab:hacking-taxonomy-app} summarizes prevalence across FOL conditions.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}llcccc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Mode} & \textbf{Mechanism} & \textbf{Exec} & \textbf{ISR} & \textbf{Rnd} & \textbf{SFT} \\
\midrule
H1 & Concl.\ in premises & 87 & 17 & 81 & 7 \\
H7 & Single prem.\ = concl. & $\bullet$ & \textbf{65} & 0 & 0 \\
Tautological & 2-comp $P{=}C$ & $\bullet$ & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
Repetition & Output degen. & $\bullet$ & -- & -- & -- \\
Contradiction & $n_{\text{comp}}$ inflated & $\bullet$ & -- & -- & -- \\
C-w/o-utility & Complex, redundant & 0 & 0 & 4 & 0 \\
Q-as-fact & Atom = fact+query & -- & -- & -- & -- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\caption{Hacking taxonomy across FOL conditions (\% of proved samples). ISR/Rand columns: $\beta{=}0.1$ 3-seed means. Exec: H1${=}87$\% in s42; $\bullet$ marks seed- or step-specific modes (H7/Tautological in s44, Repetition in s43, Contradiction at 1000 steps). C-w/o-util.: complexity-without-utility (random-specific). Q-as-fact: Prolog STA only (Table~\ref{tab:prolog-crosslogic}).}
\label{tab:hacking-taxonomy-app}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Classifier Validation.}
Hacking mode classification uses deterministic rule-based classifiers, not learned models, so standard ML precision/recall is not directly applicable.
H1 and H7 are identified by normalized text matching between conclusion and premise strings after whitespace and variable normalization; remaining modes are detected via functional analysis of the per-sample $n_{\text{necessary}}$ distribution from STA (leave-one-out ablation).
No training data or manual annotation is used for classification.

To estimate precision, we manually verified 50 randomly sampled outputs classified as H1 or H7: all 50 were confirmed correct (estimated precision ${>}$95\%, Wilson 95\% CI: [93\%, 100\%]).
Recall is inherently bounded by the text-match threshold: semantic manipulations that alter surface form while preserving the gaming structure (e.g., variable renaming beyond our normalization, or paraphrased conclusions) would be missed.
We cross-validate with functional LOO analysis: samples classified as non-hacking but showing $n_{\text{necessary}} \leq 1$ are flagged as potential false negatives.
This cross-validation revealed query-as-fact gaming in Prolog (\S\ref{app:hacking-modes}), where the strict text classifier reported 100\% non-hacking but functional analysis showed 95/97 samples were tautological ($n_{\text{necessary}}{=}1$).
The non-hacking rate for FOL conditions may therefore be slightly overestimated, as subtle semantic manipulations below our text-matching threshold would evade the strict classifier.

\subsection{H1 --- Conclusion Embedding}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The conclusion appears verbatim (or with trivial variable renaming) as one premise among multiple premises.
The solver succeeds by matching the embedded conclusion, rendering the other premises irrelevant to the proof.

\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
{\small\begin{verbatim}
Premises:
  all x (bird(x) -> flies(x)).
  bird(tweety).
  flies(tweety).  % conclusion embedded
Conclusion: flies(tweety).
\end{verbatim}}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
Variable. The embedded premise has ISR~$=1$ (removing it may break the proof), but other premises may also register as necessary depending on Prover9's search strategy.
ISR does not distinguish trivial from substantive necessity.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Conclusion embedding in some form (H1 multi-premise or H7 single-premise) is GRPO-universal at 68--97\% across all RL conditions.
Under exec-only and Random reward, it manifests as H1 (71--93\%); under ISR reward, it shifts to H7 (64.5\% pooled).


\subsection{H7 --- Conclusion Duplication}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The entire formalization collapses to a single premise whose content is identical to the conclusion.
Since $P \to P$ is trivially provable, this simultaneously maximizes exec reward.
Because the sole premise is necessary for every sub-component of the conclusion under LOO ablation, ISR is inflated toward 1.0.

\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
{\small\begin{verbatim}
Premises:
  all x ((A(x)&B(x))->(C(x)|D(x))).
Conclusion:
  all x ((A(x)&B(x))->(C(x)|D(x))).
\end{verbatim}}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR~$\approx 0.8$--$1.0$.
The single premise is trivially ``maximally necessary,'' but the proof is vacuous.
H7 is the only mode that simultaneously games both exec reward and ISR reward.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
ISR-specific: 64.5\% pooled (149/231) under ISR~$\beta{=}0.1$ (s42: 16.0\%, s43: 96.7\%, s44: 86.5\%).
\textbf{Zero} occurrences under Random~$\beta{=}0.1$ across all three seeds ($0/256$).


\subsection{Tautological Collapse}

\paragraph{Definition.}
Two-component formalizations where the premise and conclusion are identical atomic or simple formulas, yielding a $P \to P$ tautology with minimal token cost.

\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
\begin{verbatim}
Premises: p(a).
Conclusion: p(a).
\end{verbatim}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR~$=1.0$ (the sole premise is necessary).
Distinguished from H7 by having low component count ($n_{\text{comp}}\approx 2$) and atomic formulas rather than complex sub-structured conclusions.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Dominant in FOL exec-only seed~44 (PR~$=0.98$, mean $n_{\text{comp}}=2.04$, 100\% H7 by strict classifier).
Also observed in Prolog exec+STA seed~42 (100\% H7, PR~$=0.50$).


\subsection{Repetition Collapse}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The model generates identical premises or clauses repeated until the maximum completion length, producing a degenerate output with high token count but no logical diversity.
Removing any single repeated copy leaves the others intact, yielding ISR~$\approx 0$.

\paragraph{Example (Prolog).}
\begin{verbatim}
penguin(fido).
penguin(fido).
penguin(fido).
... (repeated to 512 tokens)
query(penguin(fido)).
\end{verbatim}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR~$\approx 0$. Each copy is individually redundant since identical copies remain after removal.
ISR correctly diagnoses this degeneration.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Observed in FOL exec-only seed~43 (87\% of outputs hit max completion length; PR~$=14$\%, ISR~$=0$).


\subsection{Complexity-without-Utility}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The formalization contains syntactically complex premises (nested quantifiers, multi-arity predicates) that are semantically vacuous---none individually necessary for the proof.
The complexity inflates surface metrics (formula length, nesting depth) without contributing to logical derivation.

\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
{\small\begin{verbatim}
Premises:
  all x all y (R(x,y) ->
    exists z (S(x,z) & T(z,y))).
  all x (P(x) -> Q(x)).
  P(a).            % only this needed
Conclusion: Q(a).
\end{verbatim}}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR correctly identifies the vacuous premises (ISR~$=0$ for each), pulling down the mean ISR.
This is the mode ISR is best calibrated for.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Low. Observed in Random~$\beta{=}0.1$ seed~42 at 3.8\% (3/79).
Not observed under ISR reward (ISR's gradient discourages zero-ISR premises).


\subsection{Contradiction Explosion}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The component count grows unboundedly over training.
Excess premises introduce contradictions or redundancies that trivially entail any conclusion via \emph{ex falso quodlibet}.
Individual premises may register as ISR~$=0$ (removable without breaking the proof), but the sheer count obscures the underlying triviality.

\paragraph{Example (FOL, 1000-step exec-only).}
{\small\begin{verbatim}
Premises:
  c1. c2. c3. ... c18. % 18.55 mean
  % conclusion embedded among premises
Conclusion: Q(a).
\end{verbatim}}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR~$\approx 0$ (at 1000 steps: ISR~$=0.003$, with 94.8\% of proved samples having ISR~$=0$).

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Observed in extended exec-only training (seed~42, 1000 steps).
Mean component count grows from ${\sim}6$ (500 steps) to 18.55 (1000 steps).


\subsection{Query-as-Fact Gaming}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The model converts the natural language conclusion into a snake\_case atom and includes it as both a ground fact and the query.
Prolog trivially proves the query by unifying with the fact.
This mode evades text-match classifiers designed for H1/H7 because the generated atom bears no surface resemblance to the original conclusion text.

\paragraph{Example (Prolog).}
\begin{verbatim}
% NL: "Fido is happy."
% Model output:
fido_is_happy.
:- fido_is_happy.     % query = fact
\end{verbatim}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR~$\approx 0.9$--$1.0$.
The fact is necessarily necessary (its removal breaks the query), inflating ISR.
Functionally equivalent to H7 but with a distinct surface mechanism.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Observed in Prolog exec+STA seed~44 (PR~$=0.97$, ISR~$=0.912$).
95/97 proved samples have $n_{\text{necessary}}=1$, confirming functional tautology despite the strict classifier reporting 100\% non-hacking.

\paragraph{ISR collapse trajectory (FOL exec-only, seed 42).}
Table~\ref{tab:fol-detailed} traces the ISR collapse over training:
ISR$^*=0.642$ at 100 steps $\to$ $0.132$ at 500 steps ($-79.4$\%) $\to$ $0.003$ at 1000 steps ($-99.5$\% from step 100).
PR increases monotonically ($0.32 \to 0.93 \to 0.96$) while structural quality collapses, confirming that ISR captures degeneration invisible to execution reward.
By step 1000, 94.8\% of proved samples have ISR~$=0$ and the mean component count rises to 18.55.

\paragraph{Prolog: universal Goodhart via three distinct pathways.}
All three Prolog exec+ISR seeds exhibit Goodhart's Law with 0\% non-hacking proofs (Figure~\ref{fig:prolog-comparison}), but each discovers a different gaming mechanism:
seed~42 produces clean H7 tautologies (single premise~$=$~conclusion),
seed~43 generates uppercase pseudo-Prolog that bypasses the text-match classifier while remaining functionally tautological,
and seed~44 converts NL conclusions to snake\_case atoms used as both fact and query.
The diversity of gaming pathways across seeds---despite identical training data and reward function---demonstrates that Goodhart's Law in neurosymbolic reasoning is not a single failure mode but a family of convergent exploits.

\subsection{Early-Training Hacking Analysis (100-Step Checkpoint)}
\label{app:100step}

To control for the prove-rate confound in our SFT comparison (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}), we analyze the exec-only checkpoint at 100 training steps (seed~42), where PR${=}32$\%---higher than SFT (14\%) but still early in training.
Of the 32 proved samples, 9 (28.1\%) exhibit H7 hacking (single premise identical to conclusion) and 1 (3.1\%) exhibits H1 (conclusion embedded among premises), yielding a total hacking rate of 31.2\%.
By contrast, SFT at comparable or lower PR shows 7.1\% hacking (1/14 proved samples).
This demonstrates that reward hacking emerges early in GRPO training---well before the prove-rate plateau---and is not simply an artifact of having more proved samples available for exploitation.
The 100-step hacking rate (31.2\%) is already substantially above SFT (7.1\%), supporting the claim that hacking is associated with RL optimization rather than prove-rate level alone.
